# Report for round 2

The live setup scored 0.855 on weeks 1 to 3, the mean of 3 runs per week (traces: ../traces/round-1/, one file per week per run).
Per week: week 1: 0.958 (0.875 to 1.0), week 2: 0.75 (0.5 to 1.0), week 3: 0.857 (0.857 to 0.857)

Worst week: 2. Its worst run: ../traces/round-1/week-2.run-1.jsonl
A miss in every run is a habit of the setup. A miss in one run may be chance.

## Missed: the reader acted on these, or should have, and the brief left them out
- week 3 | L061 | X @BHolmesDev | I've been thinking about what a true, closed-loop software factory will look like. | should_have | in 3 of 3 runs

## Noise the brief called important
- week 1 | L001 | X @SullyOmarr | btw ive gone back on vibe coding | noise | in 1 of 3 runs
- week 2 | L021 | X @natfriedman | 🚨 side project alert 🚨 | noise | in 2 of 3 runs
- week 2 | L023 | X @lucasmarkes__ | hairlines v0.2 is now available! | noise | in 1 of 3 runs

## Decisions it got wrong
- none

## The failure log, kept by hand

# Failure log

One entry per failure you saw with your own eyes. A rule you add to `harness/CLAUDE.md`
because of an entry carries its tag, like `(F1)`. Tagged rules can be reworded, never deleted.

<!-- Example
## F1 · week 1
Saw: the brief led with a funding round and left out the changelog entry that broke our hooks.
Expected: changes to tools I use come first.
-->

## F1 · weeks 1 to 3
Saw: the model called 15 noise links signal. Most are things made with AI: a launch video, motion
videos, landing-page shaders, design kits, new answer interfaces (L007, L015, L028, L040, L068).
Expected: I build and teach agent harnesses. A demo of what a model can make is noise to me, however
impressive. What changes how an agent is built, run or checked is what I act on.

## F2 · weeks 1 to 3
Saw: the model called hype reposts signal because their topic is harnesses or Claude Code:
"this is pure f*cking treasure" (L027), "Boris Cherny just released a prompt..." (L036),
"It is becoming f*cking dangerous" (L067).
Expected: an account repackaging someone else's work with hype is noise. I read the original.

## F3 · weeks 1 to 3
Saw: after F1 the model called three links I acted on noise. Each hands me something for my own
agent setup, though the example is a website or a gadget: Claude mods (L022), a subagent recipe
that checks a site before shipping (L059), a reverse-engineering skill (L070).
Expected: a feature, prompt recipe, skill or repo I can use in my own agent setup is signal, whatever
it is shown working on. F1 is about what a model makes, not about what an agent is used for.

# Briefing agent

You write a short weekly brief for one reader, from the links they saved that week.

The prompt names the week. Its links are in `inbox/week-N.csv` (id, date, source, title, url).
To read links, run `python3 tools/fetch.py L001 L002`, or every link of a week with
`python3 tools/fetch.py --week N`.

Write the brief in three parts, with these exact headings:

## What changed
## Who disagrees
## What to do

Cite a link by its id in square brackets, like [L014], when it matters to the reader. Leave
out the links that don't: do not list them, not even in a "skip these" line. Every id under
"What changed" or "What to do" tells the reader that link matters.

If the prompt asks about decisions, end with one line per decision, in this form:

D1: adopt
D2: wait
D3: ignore

Your reply is the brief. Write nothing before or after it.

You start in this folder, and everything you need is in it: `inbox/`, `tools/`, `cache/`.
Use paths relative to it. Never write `..`, `cd` or an absolute path: a run that reaches above
this folder is thrown away. Run one command per shell call, with no `;` or `&&` chains, because
one refused piece refuses the whole call. A refused command means only that command was
refused: `python3 tools/fetch.py` always works.

A tag in brackets after a rule, like (F1) or (R2), is a note for the person who wrote the rule.
It needs no lookup.

## What matters to this reader

The reader builds and teaches agent harnesses. Demos of what a model can make (videos,
designs, landing pages, new answer interfaces) are noise to them, however impressive. What
changes how an agent is built, run or checked is what they act on. (F1)

A post that repackages someone else's work with hype ("pure f*cking treasure", "thank me
later", "nobody noticed") is noise, even when its topic is harnesses or Claude Code. If it
points to an original by the people who did the work, the original is what matters. (F2)

A post that hands the reader something for their own agent setup (a new agent-tool feature,
a prompt or subagent recipe, a skill or repo) is signal, whatever it is shown working on: a
website, a gadget, a design. F1 is about what a model makes, not what an agent is used for. (F3)

1	## What changed
2	- Claude Code now supports mods. They change how it behaves, its UI, and its features. You write one in a few lines of TypeScript, or Claude builds it for you. Mods ship inside plugins and install with `/plugin`. This changes how you can set up and teach a harness. [L022]
3	- Kun Chen's finding is that tests an agent writes on its own haven't been shown to have value. Human guidance can change that, and he says e2e tests are the exception. He is not saying to skip tests. This bears on how you check an agent's work. [L033]
4	- Muse Gadgets is an open-source ESP32 firmware and Linux SDK. You point a coding agent at its repo to build devices. It's a ready-made repo for an agent-driven build. [L021]
5	- hairlines v0.2 ships a `/hairline-create` skill, so you can draw your own. It's a skill you could reuse. [L023]
6	
7	## Who disagrees
8	- Kun Chen is pushing back on a common habit of letting agents write their own tests. He says autonomous agent-written tests prove nothing unless a human steers them. Readers who took his post to mean "write no tests" got it wrong. [L033]
9	- The saved posts have no other real disagreement.
10	
11	## What to do
12	- Try a Claude Code mod and look at the plugin packaging. It's worth showing in your teaching. [L022]
13	- Audit any agent-written tests in your harnesses. Keep the ones a human guided, and keep e2e. [L033]
14	- Skim the Muse Gadgets repo as an example of a repo written for coding agents. [L021]
15	- Open the `/hairline-create` skill as an example of skill structure. [L023]

- Claude Code now supports mods. They change how it behaves, its UI, and its features. You write one in a few lines of TypeScript, or Claude builds it for you. Mods ship inside plugins and install with `/plugin`. This changes how you can set up and teach a harness. [L022]
- Kun Chen's finding is that tests an agent writes on its own haven't been shown to have value. Human guidance can change that, and he says e2e tests are the exception. He is not saying to skip tests. This bears on how you check an agent's work. [L033]
- Muse Gadgets is an open-source ESP32 firmware and Linux SDK. You point a coding agent at its repo to build devices. It's a ready-made repo for an agent-driven build. [L021]
- hairlines v0.2 ships a `/hairline-create` skill, so you can draw your own. It's a skill you could reuse. [L023]

## Who disagrees
- Kun Chen is pushing back on a common habit of letting agents write their own tests. He says autonomous agent-written tests prove nothing unless a human steers them. Readers who took his post to mean "write no tests" got it wrong. [L033]
- The saved posts have no other real disagreement.

## What to do
- Try a Claude Code mod and look at the plugin packaging. It's worth showing in your teaching. [L022]
- Audit any agent-written tests in your harnesses. Keep the ones a human guided, and keep e2e. [L033]
- Skim the Muse Gadgets repo as an example of a repo written for coding agents. [L021]
- Open the `/hairline-create` skill as an example of skill structure. [L023]

# Memory

One-off corrections, one line each. A correction that keeps coming back belongs in CLAUDE.md, not here.

- News about a model itself (a new or domain-trained model, a lab's finding about how a model reasons or behaves, reactions to such a finding) is noise: the reader builds the harness around the model. It is signal only if the post hands them a concrete change to how they build, run or check an agent; "this might affect evals" is not enough. (R1)

content.text:
For round 2, I added one line to `harness/memory.md`, tagged (R2). It targets the noise in week 2, which is the worst week.

**What the trace shows:** in `week-2.run-1`, the agent fetched L021 and L023, read them, and kept them under "What changed" and "What to do". It explained both through F3: "a ready-made repo for an agent-driven build" and "a skill you could reuse". But the posts themselves are a hardware SDK launch (Muse Gadgets, "point your favorite coding agent at the github repo") and a line-art pack whose skill only draws more line art. F3 is being stretched to cover products that just mention an agent or ship a skill.

**The new rule:** F3 doesn't cover a product launch whose agent or skill angle only helps make that one product. The test is whether the item would make the reader's agent better at building, running or checking any project. It goes in memory.md because the miss appeared in only one week. It should not undo F3's real cases: Claude mods (L022), the site-checking subagent recipe (L059) and the reverse-engineering skill (L070) all pass the test.

**Not addressed:** L061, the "closed-loop software factory" post in week 3, is still missed in 3 of 3 runs. The agent reads it and drops it. The post itself is only a short teaser; the full text is in an attached X article that the fetch tool doesn't return. That's a candidate for a later round.

REASON: Added a memory.md line (R2) that narrows F3: a product launch (hardware SDK, design pack) that only says "point your agent at the repo", or ships a skill for making more of that product, is noise unless it would improve the reader's agent on any project.
PREDICT: Drops the week-2 noise L021 (2/3 runs) and L023 (1/3) while keeping L022, L059 and L070 as signal; it does not fix the missed L061 in week 3.
